### Abstract

The Internet is often described as a sequence of inventions: packet switching, the TCP/IP protocol suite, hypertext, and the World Wide Web. Such a chronology is necessary but insufficient. It turns a historical outcome into a technological inevitability and leaves out the intellectual, economic, and political conditions that made the network conceivable, practicable, and socially consequential. This study proposes a different perspective: a genealogy of the twentieth-century information order. Across nine sections, it traces the movement from the postwar crisis of scientific documentation to the mathematical theory of communication; from a mechanical dream of augmented memory to packet-switched networks; from the Web's open architecture to an economy of near-zero marginal copying costs; and from media ecology to programmable privacy and, finally, to Castells's “space of flows.”

The central thesis is that the Internet emerged neither as a single device nor as the linear fulfillment of any one person's prophecy. It became a historical assemblage of at least five orders: the physical, in which signals are constrained by noise, bandwidth, and the thermodynamic cost of computation; the protocol-based, in which heterogeneous machines reach agreement without a single center; the economic, in which an expensive first copy is combined with inexpensive reproduction; the medial, in which the form of a channel alters perception and action; and the political, in which access, privacy, standards, and network inclusion become relations of power. Digitalization did not abolish scarcity. It relocated it: from copies to attention, from the availability of a message to trust in it, and from ownership of a material carrier to control over the interface, the standard, the cryptographic key, and the switching point.

**Keywords:** information; Shannon; memex; Vannevar Bush; ARPANET; Tim Berners-Lee; World Wide Web; digital economy; McLuhan; Rushkoff; cypherpunks; privacy; Castells; network society.

### Research Question

How did separate projects in information measurement, knowledge organization, network transmission, hypertext, open standards, and cryptographic privacy converge into an information order in which the Internet became technically possible and socially consequential?

### Methodology

The study combines intellectual history, contextual reading of primary technical documents, and comparative analysis of competing historiographies. Programmatic claims are tested against archives, standards, RFCs, institutional decisions, and research literature; powerful metaphors are evaluated together with the limits of their application.

### Chronological Scope

The principal period is 1945–1998, from the postwar crisis of scientific documentation and Vannevar Bush’s essay to the completion of the first edition of Castells’s trilogy on the Information Age. Earlier histories are introduced where they are necessary to explain a concept or technology.

## Academic Introduction

The title *Before the Internet* denotes not an era in which the Internet was absent as an object, but a field of preconditions in which it did not yet exist as something self-evident. By the late 1990s, most of its constituent elements had histories of their own. Information theory grew out of telephone engineering and wartime cryptography; hypertext emerged from the crisis of scientific memory and projects for augmenting intellect; packet networking arose from a combination of the Cold War, expensive computing resources, and a culture of research collaboration; the open Web developed from the practical problem of preserving connections within an international laboratory; and the digital economy drew on earlier theories of knowledge, public goods, and postindustrial society. These trajectories were not directed toward a single predetermined end. They intersected because different institutions were trying to solve different problems.

This approach requires rejecting two convenient legends. The first is technological determinism: the idea that the properties of the microprocessor generated the network society by themselves. The second is the sovereign will of the inventor: the assumption that naming one “father of the Internet” is enough to explain the network's architecture, norms, and consequences. In reality, technology and society constructed one another. Shannon's formula did not prescribe an open Web; a distributed network did not require unrestricted publication; hypertext might have become a closed commercial system; and cryptography might have remained a privilege of the state. Alternatives existed at every historical juncture.

The method combines intellectual history, analysis of primary technical documents, and comparison of competing interpretations. The ten works in the original corpus—by Shannon, Bush, Bell, Toffler, McLuhan, Negroponte, Rushkoff, Brand, Hughes, and Castells—are treated not as a canon of prophecy but as texts situated in specific historical moments. Their arguments are checked against primary papers, the CERN, DARPA/RAND, and RFC Editor archives, and bibliographic catalogs. Where a section title employs a strong metaphor, the analysis establishes its limits. “Shannon: Information Became Physics,” therefore, signifies not an identity between information and energy but the creation of a measure that was later connected to the physical irreversibility of computation. “ARPANET: The Internet Was Born of Fear” does not mean that the network was literally designed as a nuclear command-and-control system. It examines how fear of technological inferiority created an institution within which engineering objectives became broader than the military mandate.

The chronological boundaries are conventional but substantive. The year 1945 marks the publication of Bush's essay at the transition from the wartime mobilization of science to the peacetime problem of managing knowledge. The year 1998 marks the completion of the first edition of Manuel Castells's trilogy and a moment at which the network had become not merely an infrastructure but also a model of society. What changed between these dates was not simply the quantity of available information, but the grammar of its production, transmission, appropriation, and power.

## A Library Growing Faster Than Its Reader

In 1945, the problem of knowledge appeared paradoxical. Science had just demonstrated an unprecedented capacity for organization, yet its own results threatened to become inaccessible through an excess of publications. Vannevar Bush began “As We May Think” not with a hymn to the machine but with a diagnosis: specialization was useful, yet the methods for transmitting and reviewing research results were antiquated; the professional investigator could no longer keep abreast of even a restricted field (Bush, 1945). What was scarce was not the record as such. Scarcity had shifted to the ability to discover a record, the time required to read it, and the capacity to place it within a meaningful chain.

This shift matters because ordinary language conflates information with its carrier. A manuscript is scarce because it exists as a single copy; a printed book is less scarce but remains limited by print run, logistics, language, and cataloging; a digital file can be copied with almost no wear, yet its significance depends on discoverability, trust, and context. The history of the information society is therefore not a passage from absolute scarcity to absolute abundance. It is a succession of scarce links within the chain of communication.

## From Commodity to Sector

Fritz Machlup was among the first to attempt to measure the production of knowledge as part of a national economy. In *The Production and Distribution of Knowledge in the United States*, he grouped education, research, media of communication, information machines, and information services into an analytically distinct complex (Machlup, 1962). His work did not establish that earlier societies had been “non-informational.” It showed that the production, processing, and distribution of knowledge had come to occupy so substantial a share of the economy that they required separate accounting.

Marc Porat radicalized this operation in the US Department of Commerce report *The Information Economy: Definition and Measurement*. He distinguished a primary information sector, which sells information goods and services in the market, from a secondary sector: informational labor performed within organizations that produce other goods (Porat, 1977). Information thereby ceased to denote only the contents of books or telegrams; it became a function of occupations, budgets, managerial procedures, and national accounts. Yet measurement produced a methodological difficulty that remains with us. If accountants, engineers, teachers, and dispatchers all work with symbols, does that make the entirety of their work informational? The broader the definition, the more imposing the scale of the “information economy” appears—and the less discriminating the category becomes.

Daniel Bell offered a structural rather than statistical model. In *The Coming of Post-Industrial Society*, the shift from goods production to services was only the first indicator. The central “axial principle” of the new order was the primacy of codified theoretical knowledge: innovation was increasingly expected to arise from organized science, modeling, and planning, while the university and the research institute assumed a role comparable to that of the factory in the industrial era (Bell, 1973, pp. 14, 20–30). Bell carefully restricted his forecast to social structure; he did not claim that the economic, political, and cultural realms would automatically converge. That distinction must be preserved. The growing importance of knowledge does not eliminate conflict; it changes the resources over which conflict unfolds.

In *The Third Wave*, Alvin Toffler transformed these structural indicators into a sweeping civilizational metaphor. The “first wave” of agriculture, the “second wave” of industrial standardization, and the “third wave” of decentralized, demassified production form a compelling but less rigorous periodization (Toffler, 1980). Two of his observations proved especially productive: the fragmentation of a single mass audience into multiple addressable groups, and the return of the “prosumer,” who participates in producing what he or she consumes. Both would become routine features of the later networked environment. Toffler's prophetic form, however, obscures the uneven timing of change: digital production does not abolish the factory, and distributed labor often depends on centralized logistics and standardized platforms.

## An Abundance of Messages and a Poverty of Attention

Herbert Simon formulated the decisive counterthesis as early as 1971: a wealth of information creates a poverty of whatever information consumes—the attention of its recipients—and an abundance of sources therefore generates a need to allocate attention efficiently (Simon, 1971, pp. 40–41). This is not a psychological supplement to the information economy; it is its core. As copies become inexpensive, competition moves to selection. Catalogs, search engines, news feeds, rankings, and recommendations do more than help users navigate a ready-made world of messages. They allocate visibility and thereby determine which knowledge receives a chance to become action.

Four historically variable forms of information scarcity may be distinguished.

First, **scarcity of production**: reliable knowledge requires observation, experiment, labor, expertise, and time. Inexpensive copying does not make the first trustworthy formulation inexpensive.

Second, **scarcity of access**: a document may exist yet remain closed behind price, secrecy, geography, language, format, or incompatible systems.

Third, **scarcity of attention**: the volume of accessible messages exceeds the human capacity to evaluate them.

Fourth, **scarcity of trust**: the easier messages are to create and circulate, the more costly it becomes to verify their origin, integrity, and meaning. Digital signatures, reputation, peer review, and institutional authority are technologies for producing this scarce trust.

## Stewart Brand's Paradox

The phrase “Information wants to be free” is usually quoted as a moral law of digital culture. In its original context, it was more complicated. At the first Hackers Conference in 1984, Stewart Brand described a double movement: information “wants to be expensive” because it may be immeasurably valuable to its recipient, and it simultaneously “wants to be free” because the cost of distributing, copying, and recombining it is falling (Brand, 1985). The personification is rhetorical; information cannot literally “want” anything. Yet the tension is captured precisely: value and the marginal cost of a copy diverge.

In popular retellings, the first half of Brand's formulation disappeared and an observation about cost structure became a slogan. The full formulation, however, explains the persistence of conflicts over copyright, paywalls, trade secrets, and open code. The producer seeks to recover the cost of the first copy; the user sees that an additional copy costs almost nothing; the intermediary monetizes access, attention, or personal data. Artificial excludability—a password, license, technical protection measure, or contract—therefore compensates for the natural ease of reproduction.

Information became a strategic resource not because it turned into an ordinary scarce commodity. On the contrary, its political-economic force arises from the mismatch among different kinds of scarcity. Information can be nonrival in use yet enclosed by law; available in billions of copies yet invisible to a particular reader; free at the point of entry yet extraordinarily costly in its consequences. Before the mass Internet appeared, this contradiction had already been described by economists of knowledge, theorists of postindustrialism, scholars of attention, and practitioners of computer culture. The network did not create the paradox. It made the paradox an infrastructure of everyday life.
